title: Python for Data Analysis
description: Check your grip on the working environment and the compact syntax data code is written in.

lessons.title: Cells, run order, and restarting
lessons.lead: The notebook is where analysis happens — and where one specific trap costs people hours.

questions.prompt: What is displayed automatically when you run a code cell?
options: The value of the last line in the cell
Every variable assigned in the cell
Nothing unless you call `print()`
The value of the first line in the cell
questions.explain: The last expression in a cell is echoed. Everything else needs an explicit `print()`.

questions.prompt: What does the number in `In [7]` next to a cell tell you?
options: The order in which cells actually ran
The cell's position in the notebook
How many seconds the cell took
How many times the notebook has been saved
questions.explain: Cells run in whatever order you click them, not top to bottom. The counter is the only record of the real order.

questions.prompt: Which are true about a notebook's kernel?
options: All cells share one memory space
Variables from a deleted cell still exist in memory
Kernel ▸ Restart & Run All proves the notebook works from a clean start
Saving the notebook clears the variables
questions.explain: Saving does nothing to memory. Only a restart clears it — which is why you restart before sharing or submitting.

questions.prompt: "It worked before I restarted the kernel." What does that usually mean?
options: The notebook depended on a cell you had already changed or deleted
The kernel is corrupted and must be reinstalled
Jupyter needs more memory
The .ipynb file was saved incorrectly
questions.explain: State left over from an old version of a cell was holding the notebook together. Restart & Run All catches this every time.

lessons.title: One environment per project
lessons.lead: Isolation is what keeps Project A from breaking Project B — and what most "module not found" errors come down to.

questions.prompt: Which command creates a virtual environment in the current folder?
options: `python -m venv .venv`
`pip install venv`
`python venv --new .venv`
`pip freeze > .venv`
questions.explain: `-m venv` runs the built-in venv module; `.venv` is the folder it creates.

questions.prompt: You installed pandas but the import still fails. What is the most likely cause?
options: It was installed into a different environment from the one running your code
pandas is incompatible with your Python version
You need to restart the computer
pandas must be installed globally to be importable
questions.explain: Check with `python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"`, or run `!pip list` inside a notebook cell to see what the kernel can actually see.

questions.prompt: Which of these should you do with a virtual environment?
options: Activate it in every new terminal you open
Add `.venv/` to `.gitignore`
Share `requirements.txt` instead of the folder itself
Commit the `.venv` folder so teammates get the exact packages
questions.explain: The folder holds platform-specific binaries and is large. `pip freeze > requirements.txt` captures everything a teammate needs.

options: Installs every package listed in the file into the active environment
Writes the active environment's packages into the file
Upgrades pip itself
Creates a new virtual environment
questions.explain: `-r` reads the file. Writing it is the other direction: `pip freeze > requirements.txt`.

lessons.title: Loops in one line
lessons.lead: The single most recognisable piece of Python syntax in data code.

questions.prompt: Given `scores = [80, 92, 75, 41, 88]`, what does `[s for s in scores if s >= 50]` produce?
options: [True, True, True, False, True]
questions.explain: The `if` clause filters; the expression before `for` is what gets collected. 41 is dropped.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `[s * 2 for s in [1, 2, 3]]`?
questions.explain: The expression runs once per item. Repeating the list would be `[1, 2, 3] * 2`.

options: `{name: len(name) for name in names}`
`[name: len(name) for name in names]`
`(name: len(name) for name in names)`
`dict[name for name in names]`
questions.explain: Braces plus a `key: value` expression gives a dict comprehension. Braces without the colon would build a set.

questions.prompt: When should you use a normal loop instead of a comprehension?
options: When it needs several conditions and nested loops to stay readable
Whenever the list has more than 100 items
When the result is a list of numbers
Comprehensions should always be preferred
questions.explain: A comprehension is for the simple build-a-list case. Once it stops reading as one sentence, a loop is clearer.

lessons.title: The functional toolkit
lessons.lead: Four tools you will read constantly in other people's data code.

options: A small anonymous function of one expression
A loop that runs in the background
A way to import a module lazily
A type of list comprehension
questions.explain: `lambda args: expression` — the expression's value is returned automatically. No statements, no `if` blocks, no loops inside.

questions.prompt: Why does `print(map(float, ["1.5", "2.5"]))` show something like `<map object …>` instead of the numbers?
options: `map` returns a lazy iterator — wrap it in `list()` to see the values
`float` cannot be passed without a lambda
The strings must be converted before mapping
`map` only works on numbers
questions.explain: `list(map(float, raw))` materialises the results. Passing an existing function by name — `float` — is clearer than wrapping it in a lambda.

options: ['Sokha', 'Dara']
['', None]
[None, None]
It raises TypeError
questions.explain: Passing `None` as the function keeps every item that is truthy, which drops empty strings and `None`.

questions.prompt: `names` has 4 items and `scores` has 3. How many pairs does `zip(names, scores)` produce?
options: It raises ValueError
questions.explain: zip pairs by position and stops at the shortest input. The extra name is silently dropped — check your lengths first.
